The scientists who discovered and worked on electricity agreed to define the direction of current as from the positive terminal of a power supply to the negative terminal before the electron was discovered in 1897. Unfortunately, this means that conventional current is in the opposite direction to electron flow. However, not all currents are due to a flow of electrons. In a solution, or an ionised gas, positive ions flow in the direction of conventional current. Imagine a battery connected in series with a switch and a lamp. When we close the switch, we complete the circuit and the lamp lights up instantaneously, so far as our senses can tell us. How fast do you think electrons flow through the wires? The outer electrons in metal atoms are not attracted as strongly to the nucleus as those in atoms of non-metals. These electrons are free to move between all the atoms (or rather ions, because they have lost their outermost electrons) in the metal. The metal ions sit like islands in a 'sea' of free electrons, also called delocalised or conduction electrons.

The free electrons in a metal move around randomly due to their thermal energy with no overall direction to their movement. However, if a cell or battery is connected across a metal wire, the free electrons will also be pushed away from its negative terminal and pulled towards its positive terminal. The average speed at which they move in this direction is called their mean drift velocity. Mean drift velocity is small compared to the electrons' thermal velocities, but as the thermal velocities are random, they produce no overall motion of the electrons.

In a metallic conductor, the charge carriers are loosely bound to outer electrons – so-called ‘free’ or ‘delocalised’ electrons. On average, there is approximately one ‘free’ electron per atom. These ‘free’ electrons move randomly to and fro within the crystal lattice of the metal at speeds approaching one-thousandth the speed of light and are also mainly responsible for metals being good conductors of heat. When a potential difference is applied to a circuit, an electric field is created and exerts a force on the ‘free’ electrons, which causes them to ‘drift’ in the direction of the force.
